Le 28 mars dernier, Mehdi Moussaoui et J: On March 28, Mehdi Moussaoui and Jason (a pseudonym used to protect the person’s anonymity) lost their lives in a car crash in the Rosemont neighbourhood of Montréal. They were 14 and 16 years old, respectively. The deaths of the two teenagers shook the neighbourhoods of Saint-Léonard and Montréal-Nord, where they lived.
Aux alentours de 5 h 30 ce 28 mars, alor: At around 5:30 a.m. that March 28, while many Montrealers were still asleep, several gunshots rang out. Witnesses quickly reported a car whose occupants were shooting at other vehicles. A 41-year-old man was wounded in the shoulder while behind the wheel of his car, while a second man, 58, escaped unharmed. A police officer then gave chase before “losing sight” of the suspect vehicle. It was eventually found a few streets away, after crashing into a tree.
Stupéfaction ! Le premier policier sur l: Shock! The first officer on the scene found two teenagers in the vehicle. “Following the impact, one of the occupants was pronounced dead at the scene; the other occupant was reportedly taken to hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Five BEI investigators have been assigned to investigate the circumstances surrounding the intervention,” said the <l1>Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI)</l1>. According to preliminary findings, the youths appear to have targeted cars at random. No link could be established between the victims and the teenagers, nor among the victims themselves.
Si l’hypothèse d’une initiation est évoq: While police have raised the possibility of an initiation, the people close to these young people and community workers in the neighbourhoods where they lived are convinced: Mehdi and Jason were drawn into a downward spiral by bad influences, and they could have been saved.
Face à ce nouveau drame de violence par: Faced with this latest tragedy of gun violence and the young age of those involved, La Converse looked into what drives some teenagers down a tunnel of violence.
Vente illégale, fabrication par impriman: Illegal sales, 3D-printed guns, glorification on social media – weapons are now within reach of young Montrealers. It’s a reality that increasingly worries parents in at-risk neighbourhoods as tragedies multiply.
Encore sous le choc, la mère de Jason pr: Still in shock, Jason’s mother prefers to withhold her son’s identity and protect her family’s anonymity for now. That choice explains the media silence around Jason, which has caused unease in the Black community. The spotlight has instead been on Mehdi, two years his junior, whose father has spoken publicly.
Cette mère endeuillée, que nous appeller: This grieving mother, whom we will call Yolande, nonetheless shared her distress with La Converse. “They’re not just thugs with no parents and no values, that’s not true. They’re kids who met the wrong people. They were manipulated, indoctrinated by older guys, while they were vulnerable, right in the middle of adolescence and an identity crisis. I haven’t buried my son yet… I want to get through that first, but after that I’ll fight so this doesn’t happen again,” says the woman of Haitian origin.
En attendant, Yolande veut redonner une: In the meantime, Yolande wants to restore some dignity to the boy she brought into the world barely 16 years ago, and whom she never imagined she would have to lay to rest. Heartbroken, she says she was only able to see her son’s body five days after the crash, with no further explanation. “He was a much-loved little joker, generous, and he had a gift for making everyone smile. He was very athletic, he loved basketball and boxing. That’s who he was, my son,” she recalls, her voice barely above a whisper.
Ayant une sœur, un demi-frère et deux de: With a sister, a half-brother and two half-sisters, Jason was surrounded by love. He also had many friends, including Mehdi, whom he had only known for a few months, according to the family, but with whom he shared his final moments.
Proches et amis adresseront un dernier a: Family and friends will bid Jason a final farewell at a private funeral this Friday, April 12, in Montréal. On Monday, a funeral prayer was held for Mehdi at the Centre Badr mosque.
Devant l’école secondaire que fréquentai: In front of the high school Mehdi attended, his name is on everyone’s lips. Among the students who don’t dare speak, or who simply don’t know what to say, is Lina (a pseudonym), who had known him since childhood. “I’ve known him since 2014, we were about five when we became friends. He’s not a criminal, he didn’t do it for fun,” the teenager insists.
L’élève de 14 ans habitait la même rue q: The 14-year-old student lived on the same street as Mehdi. “He was a really nice boy. He was a good son and a really good big brother,” she continues. “He always took care of his mother, who has a disability. He helped her with the groceries. He was very protective of his younger brothers and sisters,” she says to illustrate her point.

En début d’année scolaire, Lina a toutef: At the start of the school year, however, Lina noticed a change in her lifelong friend’s behaviour, though she never imagined he would end up at the centre of such a tragedy. “Mehdi was very smart, but everyone knows that at that age, you’re easily influenced. He started changing when he started hanging out with the wrong people,” she says. Other students who were in class with Mehdi noticed the same thing. “He changed completely, he stopped coming to class and was acting violent at school,” Lina adds.
Les jeunes sont au courant de l’influenc: Young people are aware of the growing influence of certain groups, right down to inside their schools. Some believe Mehdi and Jason were abandoned by institutions and that individualized support could have kept them from ending up “in the wrong place at the wrong time.”
Contactée par La Converse, l’école secon: Contacted by La Converse, École secondaire Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry, where Mehdi was a student, declined to answer our questions. “In collaboration with the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal, various awareness activities take place during the school year. The school team can count on several staff members who are on the lookout for the difficulties young people are experiencing and are trained to support them,” the Centre de services scolaire de la Pointe-de-l’Île said, however.
Des jeunes qui se retrouvent dans une si: There are more and more young people in situations similar to Mehdi’s and Jason’s. From 2015 to 2020, police-reported firearm incidents in Montréal rose by 26 %, according to figures from Quebec’s Ministère de la Sécurité publique. “In fact, 56 % of perpetrators of gun violence and 38 % of victims were between 13 and 25 years old. Considering the share of this age group in the metropolitan region’s population (12 %), young people are 4.7 times more likely to be among the perpetrators of gun violence and 3.4 times more likely to be among the victims,” notes a report published in July 2023 by the International Centre for the Prevention of Crime.
Un constat que partagent largement les a: It’s an observation widely shared by community workers in the neighbourhoods hardest hit by this phenomenon. Walner Villedrouin, a youth worker with DOD Basketball, had been following Jason for three years. “The day of the crash, I had an appointment with him for his community service. I didn’t understand why he didn’t show up, it was only the next day that I found out… I don’t know exactly what he did, but he committed a delinquent act in the past, and that’s why he had to do community service. It’s a way to get them to contribute to making amends for what they did, but also to build a bond of trust that allows us to help them get out of that spiral,” he says.
Pour Jason, malheureusement, il était dé: For Jason, unfortunately, it was already too late… The youth worker mourns the death of an “intelligent kid, with values, who often came to the library to talk and even tended to talk sense into those who were tempted to do something stupid.”
Depuis un an, Walner Villedrouin note la: Over the past year, Walner Villedrouin has noticed older men hanging around the neighbourhood’s young people. In his view, criminal networks have identified how easily influenced teenagers are when they are starved for recognition and drawn to easy money. But the community sector’s very real lack of resources makes daily monitoring impossible.
Autre enjeu de compréhension de l’inquié: Another key to understanding the worrying rise in gun violence involving young people: the intercultural conflict that some youths from immigrant backgrounds cope with to varying degrees. Hocine Iratni, a social worker who works with young offenders at the CIUSSS du Centre-Sud-de-l’Île-de-Montréal, has more than 15 years of experience. “There are a lot of important factors, but what we see most among young offenders from immigrant backgrounds is that they’re going through two ruptures. One cultural, the other generational,” he explains.
Jason était originaire d’Haïti, et Mehdi: Jason was originally from Haiti, and Mehdi from Algeria. Mehdi arrived in Montréal at the age of four, so Quebec was all he had ever known. “When you’re part of a host society, it’s easier to not feel included. That feeling of exclusion, on the one hand socially, and on the other when you’re dealing with parents who lived somewhere else, creates a void in some teens. To fill that void, they’ll do anything to latch on to and belong to a group,” says Hocine Iratni.
Cette quête d’appartenance se heurte par: This quest for belonging also runs up against the generation gap with their parents. Added to this are several other important factors, such as the lure of easy money or distrust of society and institutions like the police and the media, according to the social worker. “The parents were born and raised in a completely different world. They came here and had to adapt. Their children were born here. They didn’t have to adapt, but they grew up in a different reality from the one their parents knew,” he continues.
Lorsqu’un adolescent connaît une crise,: When a teenager is going through a crisis, when their behaviour and the company they keep change, parents don’t always take the right approach. All the more so since they are generally far from imagining that the worst could happen to their children.
« On a souvent tendance à éloigner le pr: “We often tend to push the problem away from ourselves, to tell ourselves it only happens to other people,” Hocine Iratni concludes. “We have to stop thinking like that. When you’re in denial, you can’t go get help. You have to accept reality and equip yourself to prevent this kind of situation.”

Le mardi 9 avril, une dizaine de jours a: On Tuesday, April 9, about ten days after the tragedy, Beverley Jacques, director of DOD Basketball and co-founder of Coalition Pozé, an organization that fights the marginalization of young people, held a press conference in Saint-Léonard.
« Les intervenants sont fatigués, ils on: “Youth workers are tired, they need help. We don’t want these young people’s deaths to be in vain. They made bad choices, that’s undeniable, but aren’t they also victims? When it happens in the Black community, it feels like it’s normal, commonplace. We have to move past those prejudices,” said Jacques, who was named by the CBC as one of the Black changemakers in Quebec in 2023.

Celui qui connaît la famille de Jason, e: Jacques, who knows Jason’s family and had long tried to get him to play for his club, denounces a lack of resources and political will to tackle the scourge of armed crime. “We’ve been sounding the alarm for a long time. It feels like decision-makers aren’t affected because it’s not happening where they live. Once again today, we have two young people who are dead and who had access to guns instead of having a ball in their hands. We have parents who are suffering… What are we waiting for to act?” asks Beverley Jacques.
Lina Raffoul, directrice du centre Horiz: Lina Raffoul, director of the Horizon Carrière centre and the Centre Jeunesse Emploi (CJE) de Saint-Léonard, reaches the same conclusion: “We have a community of organizations that are mobilized, that work together, but that lack resources. The kids of Saint-Léonard are good kids, but a small number of them are being pursued by crime, and we have no structure to help families whose teenager is going through a crisis.”
Prêts à avoir « des discussions inconfor: Ready to have “uncomfortable but necessary discussions,” community organizations are imploring public authorities to invest more in prevention rather than repression, and to give them the means to carry out structural work instead of funding isolated projects. The goal is to protect young people from criminal networks that are stepping up their efforts to lure them in. It’s a major challenge, and one they say they are ready to take on.
<strong>« La police a tout intérêt à (re: “It’s in the police’s interest to (re)gain young people’s trust”
Plusieurs pistes d’actions à mener exist: Several possible courses of action already exist. For example, the Institut universitaire des jeunes en difficulté at the CIUSSS du Centre-Sud-de-l’Île-de-Montréal coordinates the PIVOT pilot project (Prévenir et intervenir sur les violences observées sur le territoire), as part of the Quebec government’s <l1>Stratégie québécoise de lutte contre la violence armée</l1>, known as CENTAURE. Still at the pilot stage, the project was launched in September 2023 with a budget of $1.8 million over three years. It has only been rolled out in two Montréal boroughs: Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles and Montréal-Nord.
Intervenant communautaire et chercheur à: A community worker and researcher at the Institut universitaire des jeunes en difficulté, René-André Brisebois is involved in the PIVOT pilot project. “To keep the situation from getting worse, we have to tackle the problem at its root. One of our goals is to find ways to stop or slow the impact of gun violence among young people. That includes offering opportunities for reintegration when some of them become isolated,” says Brisebois, who sees gun violence as the symptom of a deeper illness.
Plusieurs agents de PIVOT sont ainsi dép: Several PIVOT workers are thus deployed in certain schools and institutions to provide tailored support to young people most at risk of committing an act of violence. The goal is to show them that another path is possible by building a bond of trust, rather than opting for systematic repression.
Conscient de la méfiance qui existe enve: Aware of the distrust that exists toward law enforcement, René-André Brisebois believes that “it’s in the police’s interest to gain or regain the community’s trust, since everyone’s safety would be more easily achieved. Police intervention should be the last resort when dealing with a young person in difficulty.”
Il espère que les résultats seront visib: He hopes the results will be visible quickly. “PIVOT is based on results, not just good intentions. What has worked elsewhere is when the police service worked with its partners. Neighbourhood policing, community policing, builds stronger ties and trust between communities and the police – and therefore between young people and the police,” Brisebois stresses.
Aux États-Unis et en Écosse par exemple,: In the United States and Scotland, for example, two countries that have adopted this strategy on a large scale, research points to a 33 % to 50 % decrease in violent crime. A light at the end of the tunnel?
